title: Inner Product
body:
An **inner product** is the [[Dot Product]] with the specific formula thrown away and only the
rules kept. It is any operation $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$ taking two vectors from
a [[Vector Space]] to a scalar, satisfying:

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| Symmetry | $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u} \rangle$ |
| Linearity | $\langle a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = a\langle \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle + b\langle \mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\rangle$ |
| Positive definiteness | $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle \geq 0$, with equality only for $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ |

A vector space carrying one is an **inner product space**. [[Dot Product]] owns the $\mathbb{R}^n$
case and the $\cos\theta$ identity; this note owns why the abstraction is worth making.

## What you get for free

Everything geometric in the course is *defined* from the inner product rather than assumed:

$$
\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v}\rangle}, \qquad
\cos\theta = \frac{\langle \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle}{\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|}, \qquad
\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v} \iff \langle \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle = 0
$$

So length, angle, orthogonality, [[Projection]], and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality all follow
from the three rules. **Prove something using only those rules and it holds in every inner
product space at once**, including spaces whose elements are not arrows at all.

## The examples that matter here

| Space | Inner product | Where it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathbb{R}^n$ | $\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v}$ | everything, see [[Dot Product]] |
| $\mathbb{R}^n$, weighted | $\mathbf{u}^TW\mathbf{v}$, $W$ positive definite | weighted least squares, Mahalanobis distance |
| $m \times n$ matrices | $\langle A, B\rangle = \text{tr}(A^TB)$ | induces the Frobenius norm, see [[Vector Norm]] |
| Continuous functions on $[a,b]$ | $\int_a^b f(x)g(x)\,dx$ | [[Orthogonal Functions]], [[Fourier Series]] |
| $\mathbb{C}^n$ | $\overline{\mathbf{u}}^T\mathbf{v}$ | needed so $\langle \mathbf{v},\mathbf{v}\rangle$ stays real and positive |

The matrix row is the one people miss: flatten a matrix into a long vector and its dot product
with another flattened matrix is $\text{tr}(A^TB)$. **Matrices are vectors**, which is the whole
reason [[Low-Rank Approximation]] can talk about the distance between two images.

The function row is the one this degree reuses most. Replacing the sum with an integral is the
only change, and [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] is what happens when you take it seriously in
infinite dimensions.

## Related

- [[Dot Product]] (MATH 1203): the concrete case
- [[Projection]] and [[Orthonormal Basis]]: both are stated in terms of $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$
  so they transfer to functions unchanged
- [[Vector Norm]]: not every norm comes from an inner product ($L_1$ does not), which is exactly
  why $L_1$ regression has no projection formula
- [[Orthogonal Functions]] (MATH 4199): the infinite-dimensional case
